title: Needs in Moral and Political Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine two students are sharing snacks. One is simply hoping for a cookie, but the other has not eaten all day and needs food. It may be fair to help the second student first. But if there is only one snack, people may disagree about what fairness requires: should it go to the hungriest person, help the greatest number, or be shared so that everyone is equally short?
summaries.summary: The word “need” sounds powerful. If someone is hungry, unsafe, or seriously ill, it seems that something should be done. Philosophers ask whether a need by itself gives other people a moral reason to help. Some say that meeting important needs is central to morality and public policy. Others worry that need claims can be unclear: people may call many different things needs, and what helps one person may not help another. They also worry that governments could decide people’s needs for them or face an endless list of requests. In reply, philosophers suggest looking for needs that are necessary for human health, safety, independence, and participation in social life. They also distinguish a general need from its need-satisfier. Everyone may need recreation, but one person may enjoy music while another prefers walking. When there is not enough help for everyone, different rules are possible. We might help those with the greatest needs, reduce unmet need as much as possible, or try to leave people with similar unmet needs. Each rule has strengths and problems. The entry also compares needs with capabilities, meaning the real opportunities people have. Needs remain important because a person’s serious unmet need seems more urgent than a mere opportunity to buy something extra.
key_ideas: People often think unmet human needs deserve attention, but philosophers disagree about why and how strongly.
A want is not automatically a need. Needs are usually connected with avoiding harm or being able to live and participate in society.
Some needs are general, while the best way to meet them can differ between people and places.
If resources are limited, there may be no single rule that is fairest in every case.
Needs can matter in caring relationships and in justice, including questions about helping people far away or people in the future.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about needs helps us ask better questions about kindness, public services, poverty, health care, and fairness. It reminds us that treating everyone exactly alike may not be fair when people face very different problems. It also warns us to listen to people rather than letting outsiders decide everything for them. At the same time, resources are limited, so helping one person can affect what is available to others.

important_terms.definition: Something a person must have to avoid serious harm or to live and take part in life. A need is not always the same as a want.
A good reason for doing something. Philosophers ask whether a person’s need gives other people a reason, or even a duty, to help.
The things that help meet a need. People may share a need for recreation, for example, while enjoying different activities.
Fairness in how benefits and burdens are shared among people.
A need that depends on a particular goal, such as needing a paintbrush to make a painting.
A need connected with avoiding serious harm, such as needing food, water, or safety.

questions_to_think_about: How is a need different from a strong want?
If two people need help, what should we consider when deciding whom to help first?
Can people in a community help decide what counts as a need?
Should we have duties to help people in other countries or future generations?

summaries.example: Suppose a health system has enough resources either to provide a costly treatment that greatly helps one person or to provide small treatments that relieve many people’s minor conditions. A strict priority rule may focus on the person with the largest unmet need. An efficiency rule may favor the option that produces the greatest total improvement. A weighted priority rule may give extra weight to the worse-off while still considering how much treatment will help. None automatically settles every case, because fair allocation can require balancing concern for the worst-off, equal treatment, and effective use of scarce resources.
summaries.summary: The entry examines needs as reasons for action in moral and political philosophy. Ordinary need claims appear to connect facts about a person’s condition with conclusions about what others ought to do: if someone is seriously ill and needs treatment, that fact seems morally relevant. Yet philosophers disagree about whether need has irreducible normative force. On a derivative view, “A needs X” is incomplete until we identify the end Y for which X is necessary; the end, rather than need itself, does the normative work. Other views distinguish instrumental needs from categorical or basic needs, which concern avoiding serious harm and are not merely dependent on an optional project. The entry also distinguishes standing needs from presently unfulfilled needs, since a general need for sleep does not mean that a well-rested person requires immediate assistance. Even if important needs generate reasons, further questions remain about who bears the responsibility. Care relationships can create special duties, while extreme emergencies may generate duties to aid strangers. Less severe social or psychological needs may depend more heavily on existing relationships, though this is contested. Skeptics question whether needs can be identified objectively, sharply separated from socially recognized wants, or used without paternalism. Defenders respond by proposing principled accounts based on human functioning, health, autonomy, avoidance of serious harm, or minimally decent participation in a society. They also distinguish needs from their satisfiers and allow affected people a role in decision-making. key_ideas: The central dispute is whether needs have independent normative force or whether their importance derives from the ends they support.
Accounts of morally salient needs commonly connect them with serious harm, human functioning, agency, or participation in social life, but they disagree about how widely the category extends.
Need claims can be criticized as insufficiently objective, paternalistic, threatening to independence, or too demanding when resources are scarce.
A distinction between universal needs and context-dependent satisfiers explains why people in different societies may require different goods or arrangements.
Many theories of distributive justice absorb needs into broader ideas such as welfare, primary goods, resources, or disadvantage rather than treating need as an independent standard.
Under scarcity, proportional allocation, equalizing final shortfalls, maximizing need-satisfaction, weighted priority, and effectiveness each capture some values while creating trade-offs.
summaries.why_it_matters: The philosophical analysis of needs affects how we think about poverty, health care, social policy, global justice, and obligations to future people. It clarifies why equal shares may fail to treat people fairly when their needs or abilities to benefit differ. It also exposes dangers in needs-based policy: decision-makers may misidentify needs, impose unwanted assistance, or create demands that exceed available resources. Comparing needs with capabilities highlights a continuing tension between securing important conditions and protecting freedom of choice. important_terms.definition: The moral or practical force a claim has as a reason for action. The entry asks whether need claims have force independently or only because of the goals they serve.
A need for something as a means to an independently chosen goal. Needing a tool for a project does not by itself make others obligated to provide it.
A need tied to avoiding harm where the relevant purpose is treated as built into the idea of need, rather than supplied by a separate personal goal.
A general condition humans may require, such as sleep. An occurrent need is an unmet need a person has now; a dispositional need is a standing or general need.
The view that a claim is morally important only because it helps achieve some further end, such as health or social functioning.
The things, services, relationships, or conditions through which a need is met. Need-satisfiers can vary across societies and individuals.
An approach that evaluates well-being partly by people’s achieved activities and states and partly by the opportunities they have to achieve them.
A proposed way to allocate scarce resources by giving greater weight to reductions in the needs of worse-off people while also considering how much people can benefit.

questions_to_think_about: Can a need provide a moral reason independently of the goal for which an item is useful?
What principles could distinguish genuine needs from socially changing wants without ignoring cultural variation?
When should a person’s ability to benefit affect priority in distributing health-care resources?
Does respecting choice require offering options, leaving outcomes to individuals, or both?
Should obligations based on universal needs extend equally across national borders and to future generations?

summaries.example: A town has money for one project. It can repair a dangerous bridge used by a few people, improve buses used by many people, or build a recreation center that many residents strongly want. Some residents say safety is a more important need than recreation. Others ask who should decide what counts as a need and whether helping the most people is always fairest. The example shows why needs can guide public decisions but do not settle every decision by themselves.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what role needs should play in moral reasoning and political decision-making. In everyday speech, saying that someone needs food, safety, companionship, or medical care often sounds like a strong reason to help. Philosophers disagree about whether this force belongs to need itself. One side says that important needs can ground moral obligations and should guide public policy. Another side argues that need claims are incomplete: something is needed only for a further purpose, so the purpose—not “need”—explains why help is required. A useful distinction is between instrumental needs, which depend on a chosen project, and categorical needs, which concern avoiding serious harm. A person’s general need for sleep, for example, is not the same as an immediate need when that person has been awake for a day. The entry also examines relationships. Care ethics gives special importance to responding to the needs of people for whom we are responsible. However, extreme emergencies seem to require aid even when the person in danger is a stranger. Less urgent social needs may depend more on existing relationships, although philosophers disagree about this. Skeptics question whether there is an objective list of needs, since cultures and historical periods differ. They also worry that governments or experts may impose their own judgments, make people dependent, or face an endless number of expensive demands. Responses include distinguishing needs from their satisfiers, identifying needs through human health and social functioning, and involving people affected by policies in decisions. key_ideas: Philosophers disagree about whether needs have moral importance in themselves or only because they support goals such as health or participation.
Needs differ from wants, although what societies recognize as necessary can change over time.
A shared human need can have different satisfiers in different cultures, environments, or personal situations.
Needs may create special responsibilities in caring relationships, while severe emergencies may create duties to help strangers.
Critics worry that need-based policies can be subjective, paternalistic, overly demanding, or harmful to independence.
When resources are scarce, fairness may conflict with efficiency: helping the greatest number is not always the same as helping those with the strongest claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate matters whenever communities decide how to distribute limited help. It can shape views about health care, education, transportation, poverty, and international assistance. Studying it helps us avoid two mistakes: treating every want as equally urgent, or assuming that a simple needs rule solves every conflict. A good policy must consider seriousness, fairness, effectiveness, freedom, relationships, and the voices of people affected.

important_terms.definition: A condition that is necessary to avoid harm or to live a minimally decent and active life. It is usually stronger than a preference or wish.
A need for something because it helps achieve a chosen goal. A need for a particular tool may be important for a project but does not automatically create a duty for others to provide it.
A need connected with avoiding serious harm, such as a need for food, water, bodily safety, or health care.
The item, service, relationship, or condition that fulfills a need. Different people or societies may use different satisfiers for the same general need.
A moral requirement or strong reason to act. Philosophers disagree about when an unmet need creates such an obligation for another person or a government.
Fairness in distributing benefits and burdens, especially when available resources cannot meet every claim.
The idea that people’s well-being depends partly on the real opportunities they have to do and be things they value, not only on goods they possess.
A criticism that helping according to need may let officials decide what is best for people and reduce their freedom to direct their own lives.

questions_to_think_about: Should a need always count more than a strong preference? Why or why not?
Who should help when a person has an urgent need but no close relationship with the people nearby?
How can a policy respect people’s choices while still trying to meet important needs?
Is it fair to give more resources to someone who benefits less from each unit of help?
Should countries have similar duties to people outside their borders as to their own citizens?
